lessons.source_title: Doing two things / also with ~기도 하다
lessons.meaning: ~기도 하고 ~기도 하다 lists multiple facts or alternating activities, with the meaning also, sometimes or both.
lessons.when_to_use: Use it when describing two or more actions or properties together, including repeated or contrasting possibilities.
lessons.how_to_build: Attach ~기도 하다 to each relevant clause; commonly connect the clauses with ~기도 하고 and finish with ~기도 하다.
examples: 저는 아침에 차를 마시기도 하고 커피를 마시기도 해요
Sometimes I drink tea in the morning, and sometimes I drink coffee
제가 나갈 때 가끔 향수를 뿌리기도 하고 가끔 안 뿌리기도 해요
When I go out, sometimes I put on (spray) perfume, sometimes I don’t
저는 화요일에 테니스를 치기도 하고 배드민턴을 하기도 해요
On Tuesdays, sometimes I play tennis, and sometimes I play badminton
우리가 만났을 때 밥을 같이 먹기도 했고 영화를 보기도 했어요
When we met (used to meet), sometimes we would eat together, and sometimes we would watch a movie (together)

lessons.meaning: ~다고 하다 quotes a statement indirectly. The form changes with verbs, adjectives, nouns and tense.
lessons.when_to_use: Use it to report what someone said, thought or stated without repeating the exact quotation.

lessons.source_title: Asking someone to do something with 달라고
lessons.meaning: ~아/어 달라고 하다 reports a request for the speaker or another person to do something for the requester.
lessons.when_to_use: Use it when saying that someone asked for a favor or requested a particular action.
lessons.how_to_build: Attach ~아/어 달라고 to the requested verb and add 하다 or 부탁하다; conjugate the verb before 달라고.

lessons.source_title: Making or letting someone do something
lessons.meaning: ~게 하다 makes or lets somebody do something. The lesson covers causation and permission through 하다.
lessons.when_to_use: Use it when one person causes, allows or arranges for another person to perform an action.
lessons.how_to_build: Put the person or group in the appropriate object-like position, attach verb/adjective + ~게, then add 하다 and conjugate it.
examples: 저의 남자 친구가 저의 기분을 상하게 했어요
My boyfriend made me feel bad (made me ruin my feelings)
네가 그렇게 말하면 나를 창피하게 할 거야
If you say it like that, you’re going to make me ashamed

When guests come to our house, I always try to make them comfortable
저는 잘생긴 친구를 데려가서 저의 남자 친구를 질투하게 했어요
I brought a handsome man with me, so it made my boyfriend jealous

lessons.meaning: ~시키다 expresses making or having someone do an action; it is also used in many causative or lexical verbs.
lessons.when_to_use: Use it when an agent orders, causes or arranges for another person to perform an action.
lessons.how_to_build: Attach ~시키다 to the relevant noun or use the causative verb shown by HTSK; conjugate 시키다 for tense and politeness.
examples: 선생님은 학생들을 방과후 수업 시간 동안 공부시켰어요

lessons.meaning: ~(이)나 and ~거나 express alternatives, or.

lessons.how_to_build: Use ~이나 after a consonant noun and ~나 after a vowel noun. Attach ~거나 to verb or adjective stems and add the final predicate.

lessons.when_to_use: Use these expressions to qualify guesses, conclusions, appearance, respectful reference and explanations in natural Korean.

lessons.when_to_use: Use ~ㄹ/을까(요) for shall we, should I and wondering; use ~ㄹ/을게요 when promising to do something in response to the listener.

lessons.how_to_build: Use noun + 처럼. Use the appropriate verb, adjective or noun form before 듯이, including ~는 듯이 for a present action.

lessons.meaning: ~밖에 expresses nothing but or only and normally appears with a negative predicate. HTSK also covers ~ㄹ/을 수밖에 없다, have no choice but to.
lessons.when_to_use: Use it when the set of available things is limited or when an unavoidable choice is being described.
lessons.how_to_build: Place noun + 밖에 before a negative predicate. For the unavoidable construction use verb + ~(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 with the consonant rule.
examples: 오늘도 수업을 못 해서 내일부터 3일 연속으로 할 수밖에 없어요
We couldn’t do class again today, so we have no choice but to do class for three days in a row starting from tomorrow
그 커플이 매일 싸워서 사람들이 그 커플의 이혼사유를 알 수밖에 없어요
That couple fights every day, so there is no way for people to not know the reason why they got a divorce
소모품이 사무실에 아직 오지 않아서 올 때까지 기다릴 수밖에 없어요
The supplies still haven’t arrived/come to the office yet, so we have no choice but to wait until they come
그 문제를 예방할 수 없어서 또 문제가 생기면 그때 해결할 수밖에 없을 거예요
We can’t prevent that problem, so if it comes up again, we have no choice but to deal with it/fix it then

lessons.meaning: ~아/어(서) can join clauses as a connector whose subtle relationship is distinct from the ordinary cause-and-result use studied earlier.
lessons.when_to_use: Use it when the two clauses are linked in the ways explained by HTSK, including sequential or closely connected actions; do not reduce every example to because.
lessons.how_to_build: Attach ~아서 after a ㅏ/ㅗ stem and ~어서 after other vowels, with 하다 becoming 해서. Read the source examples for the context-dependent nuance.
examples: 서랍을 열어서 돈을 찾았어요

lessons.when_to_use: Use these verbs when specifying what is included in a group, list, price or statement and what is left out.
lessons.how_to_build: Use the noun as the object of 포함하다 or 제외하다 and conjugate the verb normally; the source examples show common particles and passive forms.

lessons.meaning: 상관없다 means it does not matter or it is irrelevant; 상관없이 means regardless of. HTSK combines it with ~는지, ~아/어도 and ~든.
lessons.when_to_use: Use it when saying that a choice, condition, time, place or result is irrelevant to the speaker.
lessons.how_to_build: Use a clause with ~는지, ~아/어도 or ~든 before 상관없다, or noun + 상관없이 in the middle of a sentence.

lessons.source_title: I don’t care: 신경 안 쓰다
lessons.meaning: 신경을 쓰다 means to care or pay attention, and 신경을 안 쓰다 means not to care. The lesson treats 신경 as a noun.
lessons.when_to_use: Use it for caring about a noun, a clause, a question or a condition, especially in the common negative form.
lessons.how_to_build: Use noun + 에 대해 신경을 쓰다/안 쓰다. Use ~는 것, ~는지 or ~아/어도 before the expression for clauses and conditions.
examples: 나는 네가 어디 가는지 신경을 안 써
